final_proof:
Let \(D_f:\mathcal P(S_1)\to\mathcal P(S_2)\) denote the direct-image map \(D_f(A)=f[A]\). To say that \(D_f\restriction_{\tau_1}\) is a surjection from \(\tau_1\) to \(\tau_2\) means precisely that
\[
\tau_2=\{f[U]:U\in\tau_1\}.
\tag{*}
\]

First suppose that \((S_2,\tau_2)\) is a topological space homeomorphic to \(T_1=(S_1,\tau_1)\). Let \(f:S_1\to S_2\) be a homeomorphism. Then \(f\) is bijective, and both \(f\) and its inverse map \(f^{-1}:S_2\to S_1\) are continuous.

If \(U\in\tau_1\), then
\[
f[U]=(f^{-1})^{-1}[U],
\]
where the right-hand side is the inverse image of \(U\) under the inverse map. By continuity of \(f^{-1}\), it follows that \(f[U]\in\tau_2\). Thus \(D_f\) maps \(\tau_1\) into \(\tau_2\).

Conversely, if \(V\in\tau_2\), continuity of \(f\) gives \(f^{-1}[V]\in\tau_1\), and bijectivity gives
\[
f[f^{-1}[V]]=V.
\]
Thus every member of \(\tau_2\) is the direct image of a member of \(\tau_1\). Hence \(D_f\restriction_{\tau_1}:\tau_1\to\tau_2\) is surjective.

For the converse, suppose that there is a map \(f:S_1\to S_2\) satisfying conditions (1) and (2). Thus \(f\) is bijective and equality (*) holds. We first prove that \(\tau_2\) is a topology on \(S_2\).

Since \(\varnothing,S_1\in\tau_1\), equality (*) gives
\[
\varnothing=f[\varnothing]\in\tau_2
\quad\text{and}\quad
S_2=f[S_1]\in\tau_2,
\]
the latter equality following from surjectivity of \(f\).

Let \((V_i)_{i\in I}\) be any family of members of \(\tau_2\). Put \(U_i=f^{-1}[V_i]\). By (*) and bijectivity, each \(U_i\) belongs to \(\tau_1\) and \(V_i=f[U_i]\). Therefore
\[
\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i
 =\bigcup_{i\in I}f[U_i]
 =f\left[\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\right].
\]
Because \(\tau_1\) is a topology, \(\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau_1\), so (*) implies that \(\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i\in\tau_2\).

If \(V,W\in\tau_2\), write \(V=f[U]\) and \(W=f[Z]\) for some \(U,Z\in\tau_1\). Since \(f\) is injective,
\[
V\cap W=f[U]\cap f[Z]=f[U\cap Z].
\]
Now \(U\cap Z\in\tau_1\), so (*) gives \(V\cap W\in\tau_2\). Closure under all finite intersections follows by induction, with the empty finite intersection already covered by \(S_2\in\tau_2\). Hence \(\tau_2\) is a topology on \(S_2\).

It remains to show that \(f\) is a homeomorphism. If \(V\in\tau_2\), then (*) and bijectivity imply that \(f^{-1}[V]\in\tau_1\); therefore \(f\) is continuous. Let \(g:S_2\to S_1\) be the inverse map of \(f\). For every \(U\in\tau_1\),
\[
g^{-1}[U]=f[U]\in\tau_2
\]
by (*). Hence \(g\) is continuous. Thus \(f\) is a homeomorphism from \((S_1,\tau_1)\) to \((S_2,\tau_2)\), proving the converse and therefore the equivalence.
